nameStory: The twice-stabbed lady beetle gets its dramatic name from the two bright red spots on its black wing covers, which look like vivid drops of blood against its shiny dark body. These crimson 'stab wounds' make this native North American beetle instantly recognizable among its more colorful cousins.
description: The twice-stabbed lady beetle is a small, dome-shaped beetle with a striking black and red color pattern that's the reverse of what most people expect from ladybugs. Instead of red with black spots, this species sports a glossy jet-black body with exactly two bright red spots — one on each wing cover. Like other lady beetles, it's a beneficial predator that helps control garden pests, but its gothic coloration makes it stand out in any insect collection.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Shiny jet-black wing covers with exactly two bright red circular spots, one centered on each wing cover — no other spots or markings

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Glossy, almost mirror-like black surface that feels smooth and hard to the touch, reflecting light like polished plastic

idTips.label: Abdomen Color
idTips.description: When the wing covers are lifted or the beetle is viewed from below, the abdomen appears yellow or reddish, contrasting with the black thorax

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Classic dome-shaped lady beetle profile — rounded and convex like a tiny black helmet with a smooth, curved outline

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and compact, roughly the size of a pencil eraser, fitting comfortably on a fingertip without overlapping the edges

habitat: Look for twice-stabbed lady beetles in gardens, orchards, and forest edges throughout New England, especially on trees and shrubs where they hunt for scale insects and aphids. They're particularly fond of conifers like pine and spruce, but also visit deciduous trees and can be found on roses, fruit trees, and other woody plants where their prey congregates.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin actively hunting on warming tree branches and garden plants, often seen crawling on bark in sunny afternoon spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting prey and mating, with new larvae developing on infested plants throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into autumn, building up energy reserves before seeking shelter, often clustering on tree trunks during warm October days.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under loose bark, in leaf litter, or other protected spots, occasionally emerging on unusually warm winter days to bask in sunny locations.

funFact: Unlike most lady beetles that primarily eat aphids, twice-stabbed lady beetles are specialist scale hunters — they can completely clean a tree branch of armored scale insects that other predators can't even penetrate, making them like tiny black ninjas with a very specific set of skills.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the two-stabbed lady beetle (Chilocorus orbus), which is nearly identical but mainly found in California. In New England, the twice-stabbed is your only shiny black lady beetle with exactly two red spots, making identification relatively straightforward.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'twice-stabbed' can be confusing since there's also a 'two-stabbed' lady beetle — they're different species with nearly identical appearances but different ranges. Some people also call any dark lady beetle a 'twice-stabbed,' but true twice-stabbed lady beetles always have exactly two red spots, never more or fewer.
compareHints: This is the only Chilocorus species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other black lady beetles in the region, twice-stabbed lady beetles are distinguished by having exactly two red spots rather than multiple spots, and by their particularly glossy, mirror-like finish that's shinier than most other dark-colored lady beetle species.
